Pilar 9 — Diffusion Models for Soil-Map Patches

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/pilar9-diffusion-models.Rmd
pilar9-diffusion-models.Rmd

Abstract

Every method in this package so far answers “what is the soil property here?” with a mean and, if you are lucky, an interval. None of them answers a question soil scientists actually ask: what does a plausible soil landscape look like? A per-pixel interval cannot answer it, because the pixels are not independent — a map assembled from per-pixel quantiles is smoother than any real landscape and belongs to no coherent realisation.

Pillar 9 samples whole maps. It implements a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (Ho et al. 2020) over soil-map patches: a generative model whose draws are joint realisations, each internally consistent in a way marginal quantiles never are.

1. The forward process is fixed, only the reverse is learned

The construction is unusual among generative models in that half of it has no parameters at all.

Forward. Take a real patch x0x_0 and destroy it over TT steps by adding Gaussian noise on a fixed schedule β1,…,βT\beta_1, \dots, \beta_T:

q(xt∣xt−1)=N(1−βtxt−1,βtI). q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = N\!\big(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\; \beta_t I\big).

Writing αt=1−βt\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t and α‾t=∏s≤tαs\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s, the steps telescope into a closed form — you can jump to any noise level in one shot, which is what makes training cheap:

q(xt∣x0)=N(α‾tx0,(1−α‾t)I). q(x_t \mid x_0) = N\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\; (1 - \bar\alpha_t) I\big).

Reverse. The only learned object is a denoiser ϵθ(xt,t)\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) trained to recover the noise that was added. Because the forward step is Gaussian with small βt\beta_t, the reverse step is also approximately Gaussian, and its mean is available in closed form once ϵθ\epsilon_\theta is known.

The training objective reduces to plain regression:

ℒ(θ)=𝔼x0,t,ϵ[∥ϵ−ϵθ(α‾tx0+1−α‾tϵ,t)∥2]. \mathcal{L}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\,t,\,\epsilon} \Big[\big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\; t\big)\big\rVert^2\Big].

No adversarial game, no discriminator, no mode collapse — the loss is a mean squared error against a target you generated yourself.

1.1 The schedule

edaphos uses the cosine schedule of Nichol and Dhariwal (Nichol and Dhariwal 2021) rather than the original linear one, because a linear schedule destroys small patches too early and wastes most of the trajectory on pure noise.

sch <- dm_cosine_schedule(T = 100L)

str(sch, max.level = 1)
#> List of 6
#>  $ T                      : int 100
#>  $ alphas                 : num [1:100] 0.999 0.999 0.998 0.998 0.997 ...
#>  $ betas                  : num [1:100] 0.000531 0.001117 0.001603 0.002089 0.002577 ...
#>  $ alphabar               : num [1:100] 0.999 0.998 0.997 0.995 0.992 ...
#>  $ sqrt_alphabar          : num [1:100] 1 0.999 0.998 0.997 0.996 ...
#>  $ sqrt_one_minus_alphabar: num [1:100] 0.0231 0.0406 0.057 0.073 0.0888 ...

# alphabar is the signal that survives to step t
round(sch$alphabar[c(1, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100)], 4)
#> [1] 0.9995 0.9722 0.8471 0.4939 0.1443 0.0000

α‾t\bar\alpha_t decays monotonically from ~1 (the patch is intact) to ~0 (pure noise). The cosine shape keeps signal alive through the middle of the trajectory, which is where most of the learning happens.

2. Real patches from the Cerrado grid

br_cerrado is a 45 × 45 regular grid, so it can be reshaped into an image and cut into overlapping patches — real spatial structure, no simulation.

Which layer to model is not arbitrary. A generative model of a spatial field can only learn structure the field actually has, so measure that first:

data(br_cerrado)

g  <- 45L
ux <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$x)); uy <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$y))

as_grid <- function(v) {
  m <- matrix(NA_real_, g, g)
  m[cbind(match(br_cerrado$x, ux), match(br_cerrado$y, uy))] <- v
  m
}

# Lag-1 spatial autocorrelation, averaged over rows and columns.
lag1 <- function(p) {
  h <- stats::cor(as.vector(p[, -ncol(p)]), as.vector(p[, -1]))
  v <- stats::cor(as.vector(p[-nrow(p), ]), as.vector(p[-1, ]))
  (h + v) / 2
}

vapply(c("soc", "twi", "elev", "map_mm"),
       function(nm) lag1(as_grid(br_cerrado[[nm]])), numeric(1))
#>       soc       twi      elev    map_mm 
#> 0.2304873 0.7848433 0.9396653 0.9684636

soc in this synthesised grid is close to white: it is generated as a function of the covariates plus independent noise, so once you look at an 8 × 8 window there is little left for a spatial model to learn. (The Pillar 7 vignette reaches the same conclusion from the other direction.) We therefore model twi, the topographic wetness index — a standard DSM covariate and a soil-water proxy — which does carry short-range structure.

field   <- as_grid(br_cerrado$twi)
# The denoiser works on zero-mean, unit-scale fields.
field_z <- (field - mean(field)) / stats::sd(field)

P <- 8L                                   # patch size
starts <- seq(1L, g - P + 1L, by = 3L)
grid   <- expand.grid(r = starts, c = starts)

stack <- array(0, dim = c(nrow(grid), P, P))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
  r <- grid$r[i]; cc <- grid$c[i]
  stack[i, , ] <- field_z[r:(r + P - 1L), cc:(cc + P - 1L)]
}

c(n_patches = dim(stack)[1],
  sd        = mean(apply(stack, 1L, stats::sd)),
  lag1      = mean(apply(stack, 1L, lag1)))
#>   n_patches          sd        lag1 
#> 169.0000000   0.5957468   0.3435722
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 1.4, 0.4))
for (i in c(1, 20, 60, 110))
  image(stack[i, , ], axes = FALSE, main = sprintf("real #%d", i),
        col = hcl.colors(32, "Terrain2"))

par(op)

3. Training the denoiser 

fit <- dm_fit(
  stack   = stack,
  backend = "r",   # reference path, so the vignette knits with no libtorch
  T       = 100L,
  epochs  = 250L,
  hidden  = 48L,
  lr      = 0.02,
  seed    = 1L
)
#> [dm_fit] backend = 'r' is a reference sampler whose draws are over-dispersed and spatially incoherent (not calibrated to the field's spatial statistics); use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) for coherent samples.

length(fit$history)
#> [1] 250
round(utils::tail(fit$history, 3), 5)
#> [1] 0.87110 0.87930 0.87186

The loss is the score-matching MSE above. It should fall and then flatten; it does not go to zero, and should not — the target ϵ\epsilon is irreducibly random.

4. Sampling

dm_sample() runs ancestral sampling: start from xT∼N(0,I)x_T \sim N(0, I) and step down to t=0t = 0, subtracting the predicted noise and re-injecting a smaller amount at each step.

gen <- dm_sample(fit, n_samples = 4L, seed = 7L)
dim(gen)
#> [1] 4 8 8
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 1.4, 0.4))
for (i in 1:4)
  image(gen[i, , ], axes = FALSE, main = sprintf("generated #%d", i),
        col = hcl.colors(32, "Terrain2"))

par(op)

5. Judging a generative model honestly

“They look plausible” is not a result. A generative model of spatial fields makes a checkable claim: the spatial statistics of its draws should match those of the training data. Two summaries are enough to catch the common failure modes.

gen_many <- dm_sample(fit, n_samples = 40L, seed = 99L)

summarise <- function(a, lbl) {
  data.frame(
    set  = lbl,
    sd   = sprintf("%.3f", mean(apply(a, 1L, stats::sd))),
    lag1 = sprintf("%.3f", mean(apply(a, 1L, lag1)))
  )
}

rbind(summarise(stack,    "real patches"),
      summarise(gen_many, "generated"))
#>            set    sd   lag1
#> 1 real patches 0.596  0.344
#> 2    generated 3.032 -0.020

sd catches a sampler that has collapsed towards the mean field or, in the other direction, one that is diverging. lag1 is the one that matters here: it asks whether neighbouring cells in a generated patch co-vary the way they do in the data. A model that matches the marginal histogram while emitting spatially incoherent noise scores near zero.

Read the table. The generated lag1 is approximately zero against roughly 0.34 in the data, and the generated sd is several times too large. The pure-R backend has learned the marginal scale of the field only: it is producing over-dispersed noise, not soil landscapes.

That is a real, reproducible negative result, and it is reported here rather than hidden behind four plausible-looking thumbnails. Section 6 explains why, and Section 7 what to do about it.

6. Why: what the R backend actually trains

With backend = "r" — requested explicitly here so the vignette knits with no system dependencies (the package default is "auto", which uses torch when libtorch is present and falls back to this R path otherwise) — the denoiser’s hidden layers are randomly initialised and frozen; only the readout layer is fit. That is an Extreme Learning Machine regime (Huang et al. 2006): fast, dependency-free, genuinely trained, and far less expressive than a full network.

The loss tells you this directly, once you know what to compare it to. The target ϵ\epsilon is standard normal, so a denoiser that predicts nothing at all — ϵθ≡0\epsilon_\theta \equiv 0 — scores a mean squared error of exactly 1:

c(final_loss    = utils::tail(fit$history, 1),
  trivial_loss  = 1)
#>   final_loss trivial_loss 
#>    0.8718602    1.0000000

The gap between the two is all the structure the model has captured. Adding epochs does not close it: the readout has already converged, and random features cannot represent the score of a spatially correlated field.

7. The torch backend

backend = "torch" trains every layer by autograd, which is what the architecture needs to learn a spatial score function:

fit_t <- dm_fit(stack, T = 200L, epochs = 1500L, hidden = 128L,
                lr = 1e-3, backend = "torch", device = "cpu", seed = 1L)
gen_t <- dm_sample(fit_t, n_samples = 40L, seed = 99L)

c(sd = mean(apply(gen_t, 1L, stats::sd)),
  lag1 = mean(apply(gen_t, 1L, lag1)))

This chunk is not evaluated when the vignette is built, because torch is a Suggests dependency and the vignette must knit without it. Run it yourself and apply the same §5 diagnostic — the two-number check is the point, and it should be applied to whichever backend you deploy, not taken on trust from this document.

8. Conditional generation

Passing conditioning makes the sampler produce patches consistent with covariates rather than draws from the unconditional prior — the route to “simulate this landscape given this climate”.

elev <- as_grid(br_cerrado$elev)

cond <- matrix(0, nrow(grid), 1L)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
  r <- grid$r[i]; cc <- grid$c[i]
  cond[i, 1L] <- mean(elev[r:(r + P - 1L), cc:(cc + P - 1L)])
}
cond[, 1L] <- as.vector(scale(cond[, 1L]))

fit_c <- dm_fit(stack, conditioning = cond, backend = "r", T = 100L,
                epochs = 250L, hidden = 48L, lr = 0.02, seed = 1L)

low  <- dm_sample(fit_c, n_samples = 12L,
                  conditioning = matrix(-1.5, 12L, 1L), seed = 3L)
high <- dm_sample(fit_c, n_samples = 12L,
                  conditioning = matrix( 1.5, 12L, 1L), seed = 3L)

c(mean_low_elev  = mean(low),
  mean_high_elev = mean(high))
#>  mean_low_elev mean_high_elev 
#>     -0.1867973     -0.2085048

If conditioning is doing anything, these two differ in the direction of the elevation–carbon relationship in the training grid. With an ELM readout and a 100-step schedule the effect is modest; treat this as a demonstration of the interface rather than a calibrated conditional simulator.

9. Limitations

  • The pure-R backend does not produce spatially coherent samples (§5, §6). It is a correct implementation of the DDPM algorithm with a denoiser too weak to learn the score of a spatial field. Treat it as a reference implementation and a test bed for the interface, not as a generative model you would publish from.
  • Patches are 8 × 8. Real soil landscapes have structure at scales this window cannot represent.
  • Overlapping patches cut from one 45 × 45 grid are not independent training examples; the effective sample size is far below dim(stack)[1].
  • Nothing here stitches patches into a seamless map. Tiling generated patches produces visible seams — patch-to-map assembly is not implemented.
  • The denoiser is an MLP over the flattened patch, not a 2-D U-Net, so it has no translation-equivariant inductive bias. This is the main architectural gap between this pillar and the diffusion literature.
  • br_cerrado is synthesised, and §2 models twi rather than a soil property because soc in this grid is near-white at patch scale. This vignette demonstrates the sampler and its diagnostic, not a finding about Cerrado soils.

References

Ho, Jonathan, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel. 2020. “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 6840–51.
Huang, Guang-Bin, Qin-Yu Zhu, and Chee-Kheong Siew. 2006. “Extreme Learning Machine: Theory and Applications.” Neurocomputing 70 (1–3): 489–501. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2005.12.126.
Nichol, Alexander Quinn, and Prafulla Dhariwal. 2021. “Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.” Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning 139: 8162–71.
